classicBeybladePhysics: Classic Plastic Generation physics apply: physical Beyblades stay palm-sized, solid and tip-driven; right-spin and left-spin remain constant; stadium translation is separate from axial rotation; collisions use direct Attack Ring contact with recoil; supernatural energy remains anchored to the visible physical top. Real-world spin-stability lock: angular momentum is the only thing that keeps a free Beyblade balanced on its pointed tip. As RPM approaches zero, precession must widen, the rim or base must touch, and gravity must tip the body onto its side. A non-spinning free top may not remain upright on its tip or freeze in a balanced pose. It may stay level while not spinning only when visibly supported by a hand or fixture, lying flat on a broad surface, or firmly locked to both launcher posts. Observable Beyblade dynamics lock: every active top is a rigid palm-sized gyroscope with one tip in continuous contact with the stadium after landing. High RPM produces rapid circumferential texture blur around the Attack Ring; center emblems may remain centered but perimeter markings may not stay crisp or frozen. The contact tip and center of mass define one coherent axis; the top never hovers. Any tilt produces continuous gyroscopic precession: the lean direction rotates around the contact point and may damp toward vertical at high RPM or widen as RPM falls, but it never freezes at one lean angle or compass direction. Tip friction, gravity, and the bowl tangent create a continuous curved trajectory with position continuous from frame to frame; tops do not hold a staged side-by-side formation, teleport, or pivot on a glued point. Each collision is a brief Attack-Ring-to-Attack-Ring impulse followed immediately by visible separation, tangential deflection or rebound, changed travel velocity, wobble, and some speed loss; tops never overlap, stick together, or cluster like magnets. Mechanical energy then decreases monotonically through friction and impacts: orbit speed and RPM decay, precession widens, the rim or base may scrape, and a fully stopped unsupported top falls onto its side. Preserve every owner's authored top design, axial spin direction, path, and outcome across cuts.

stadiumMotionLock: Post-landing stadium-motion lock: after the tip's first contact, a spinning Beyblade must continue both axial rotation and visible translation across the bowl. A brief landing skid transitions immediately into a curved orbit governed by tip friction, gravity and the local bowl tangent; on a slope it travels along or down the surface and may precess, climb, descend or deflect, but it never adheres to the slope, freezes in place, or pivots around a glued point. Even a defense-type top traces a tight low-speed orbit or small precessing circle. It may become stationary only after RPM decays, wobble widens, the rim scrapes and the body falls onto its side.

rotationalCausalityLock: Rotational-causality lock: spin energy comes from the ripcord-driven launcher gear while the top is still mechanically engaged. Before the pull the loaded top is stationary. During the pull it accelerates while remaining flush-mounted; on every successful release, the very first unsupported airborne frame already shows rapid high-RPM axial rotation and strong circumferential Attack Ring blur. The top carries that same continuous rotation through tip-first landing, with no stopped, crisp, or low-RPM airborne or landed interval followed by a later spin-up. After detachment its RPM may persist briefly, transfer through a visible rim impact, or decrease through drag, friction, scraping and collision, but it never increases or restarts without a photographed external torque. An explicitly failed release that receives no usable launcher torque remains non-spinning, falls under gravity, and never starts spinning by itself.
